title: Writing Clear Prompts: Task, Context, Format, Examples

thumbnail.headline: Same Tool, Better Prompt
thumbnail.image: Navy background, two chat bubbles side by side: a short vague one with a grey cross and a four-line one with a teal tick, headline in teal Inter Bold.

slide.title: Same Tool, Better Prompt
slide.body: Left: short chat bubble 'Write a notice…' with grey cross. Right: four-line bubble labelled Task · Context · Format · Example with teal tick. Small tag: AI for Everyday Work · Lesson 2.

production_notes: [VERSION] Screen demo tool: Claude (free tier) in a web browser, as named in the course brief; ChatGPT free tier is the backup. Check the live interface (starting a new chat, window layout) before recording.
Screen demo lesson (approved 2026-09-23): scenes 9 to 13 are screen recordings. Use two browser windows side by side for scene 12.

The AI answers in the demo will differ from the lesson text. Record the vague answer first and point out any invented or missing details it really contains; if it happens to invent none, say so in the edit and keep the comparison on length and tone.
Amara and her Lagos company are hypothetical. Use a demo account with no personal data visible in the sidebar or chat history.
Both prompts are shown in full on code-layout slides (scenes 8 and 10) so learners can pause and copy them.

Hook.voiceover: Two people ask the same AI assistant for a notice about the office move. One gets a vague, generic text that needs rewriting. The other gets a draft she can send after a few small edits. The tool is the same. The difference is the prompt.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, we saw what an AI assistant is good at. Today we learn how to ask it clearly. A prompt is the instruction you type. The assistant only knows what is in your prompt and in the conversation so far. If you leave out important details, it fills the gaps with guesses.

slide.title: What is a prompt?
slide.body: Speech bubble 'Your prompt' → assistant icon. Empty gaps in the bubble are filled with question marks labelled 'guesses'.

Explain.voiceover: A clear prompt has four parts. First, the task, what you want the assistant to do. Use a clear verb, such as write, summarise, list or compare. Second, the context, the background it needs. Who is the reader? What is the situation? What are the key dates and places?

slide.title: Four parts of a clear prompt
slide.body: 1. Task: a clear verb (write, summarise, list, compare) · 2. Context: reader, situation, key facts · 3. Format (greyed) · 4. Example (greyed)

Explain.voiceover: Third, the format, what the answer should look like. For example, an email of about one hundred and twenty words, five bullet points, or a friendly and simple tone. Fourth, an example, if you have one. An old notice that worked well helps a lot.

slide.title: Four parts of a clear prompt
slide.body: 1. Task · 2. Context · 3. Format: length, layout, tone · 4. Example: an old notice or a sentence in the style you like

Explain.voiceover: Think of it like briefing a temporary colleague who has just arrived. If you only say do the notice, they will guess. If you tell them what it is about, who will read it and how long it should be, they can do good work the first time.
Explain.stock_query: manager briefing new colleague at desk
Explain.on_screen_text: Brief it like a new colleague

Explain.voiceover: You do not always need all four parts. A quick question may only need a task. But for anything you will send to other people, context and format usually give a much better first draft. And you can continue the conversation. If the answer is too long, just ask for a shorter one.

slide.title: How much do you need?
slide.body: Quick question → Task only. Anything you send to others → Task + Context + Format (+ Example). Footer: You can always follow up: 'Make it shorter.'

Explain.voiceover: One safety rule from lesson one still applies. Your context must not include confidential or personal data. Use general descriptions, such as our team of forty staff, instead of names and private details.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's try it. Amara is an office manager in Lagos, in Nigeria. Her company is moving to a new floor, and she must tell the staff. I'm using the free version of Claude in a web browser.
Demonstrate.stock_query: office manager packing boxes office move

Demonstrate.voiceover: Here is her first prompt. It is one short sentence, with no details at all.

slide.title: The vague prompt
slide.body: Write a notice about the office move.

Demonstrate.voiceover: I open a new chat, type the vague prompt and press Enter. Look at the answer. It is long and very general. It may also invent details that are not true, such as a move to a new city.
screen_steps: Open Claude (free tier) in a web browser and start a new chat
Type 'Write a notice about the office move.' and press Enter
Highlight any invented or missing details, for example a new city location or no date

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now the improved prompt, with the four parts on separate lines. The task is a notice to staff. The context gives the facts: from the third floor to the seventh floor, on Friday, desks packed by Thursday at four, boxes at reception. The format is a friendly email of about one hundred and twenty words. And the example is an opening line.

slide.title: The improved prompt
slide.body:
Task: Write a notice to staff about our office move.
Context: We move from the 3rd floor to the 7th floor of the same building on Friday. Staff must pack their desks by Thursday at 4 p.m. Boxes are at reception.
Format: An email of about 120 words, friendly and clear, with the key dates in bold.
Example: Start like this: "Good news: we are moving up!"

Demonstrate.voiceover: I open a second new chat, so the first answer does not influence this one. I type the improved prompt, one part per line, and press Enter.
screen_steps: Type the improved prompt with Task, Context, Format and Example each on its own line
Press Enter and wait for the answer

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now let's put the two answers side by side. The second one uses the correct floors and dates. It is the right length, and the tone is friendly. The first one is longer and guesses.
screen_steps: Place the two chats in two browser windows side by side
Highlight the correct floors and dates in the second answer
Compare the length of the two answers
Point to the friendly opening line in the second answer

Demonstrate.voiceover: I don't need to start again to improve it. In the second chat I type a follow-up, make it twenty words shorter, and the assistant rewrites the draft.
screen_steps: In the second chat, type 'Make it 20 words shorter.' and press Enter

Demonstrate.voiceover: Amara still checks the dates, changes one sentence so it sounds like her, and then sends it. A common mistake is to write a very short prompt and then decide that AI is not useful. Before you press Enter, ask yourself: would a new colleague understand this request?

slide.title: Before you press Enter
slide.body: "Would a new colleague understand this request?"

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a clear prompt has four parts: task, context, format and, if you have one, an example. Second, the more relevant context you give, the fewer guesses the assistant makes, but never include confidential or personal data. Third, you can improve an answer by continuing the conversation, for example make it shorter, or use a more formal tone.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Task · Context · Format · Example. 2. More context, fewer guesses (no confidential data). 3. Improve by following up: 'Make it shorter.'

CTA.voiceover: Your turn. In the exercise below this video, take the vague request, write a notice about the new parking rules, and rewrite it with the four parts. Invent the details and use no real names. Compare the two answers and note three differences. The next lesson is Safe Use at Work: Privacy and Confidential Data. See you there.
